analysis.one_liner: Repeals the entire Affordable Care Act in a single sentence.
analysis.headline: The one-sentence repeal bill died in the Senate Finance Committee with zero cosponsors and never came to a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Sen. David Vitter introduced a bill that would erase the entire Affordable Care Act — the 2010 health care law — with a single line of text repealing it and every amendment it made. The bill was read once in the Senate and referred to the Finance Committee, which never acted on it. It had no cosponsors and never reached the Senate floor.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main winners would have been health insurers and employers freed from the law's coverage requirements, and the highest earners and largest estates, who would no longer owe the law's added Medicare taxes. People with preexisting conditions, low- and middle-income families receiving help paying for coverage, and young adults on their parents' plans would have lost those protections and benefits.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act and all amendments made by that Act, in a single provision [S2][S3].
Repeal would remove the law's requirements on insurers and employers, leaving health coverage rules as they stood before 2010.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would have fallen on the people the law helped: those who gained coverage or protections under it, including people with preexisting conditions and families receiving subsidies, would have lost them, while the tax burden the law placed on high earners and affected industries would be lifted.
analysis.who_pays_short: People relying on ACA coverage protections

drawbacks.text: The bill is a bare repeal with no replacement provisions, so everything the ACA established — including coverage protections and subsidies — would end at once with nothing taking its place [S2][S3].
Supporters of repeal argued the law imposed mandates and costs on individuals, employers, and insurers; the bill offered no findings or alternative plan of its own [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit runs to industries and high earners relieved of the law's rules and taxes; its cost runs to the millions of people who had gained coverage, subsidies, or protections under the law, who would lose them with nothing offered in exchange. As written, it is a one-sentence repeal with no transition or replacement, so the losses would be immediate and unmitigated.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never considered it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. David Vitter introduced the bill on March 22, 2010 [S1][S5].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance [S5].
No further action was taken before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, so the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Affordable Care Act remained law, so the people who benefited from its coverage expansions and protections kept them. Nobody gained from the bill's death beyond the status quo; the repeal effort itself gained nothing but a stated position.

for.name: Sen. David Vitter
for.role: U.S. Senator from Louisiana; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and put it forward for repeal of the Affordable Care Act.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its referral; it was never considered or reported.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican sponsored the bill to repeal a law passed by a Democratic Congress, and no member of either party cosponsored it [S4][S5].

industries.note: Repeal would free insurers from the ACA's coverage rules and minimum-loss-ratio requirements, but would also end the mandate-driven enrollment and subsidies that brought them new customers. The bill itself does nothing to structure their role either way [S2][S3].
The ACA imposed rebates and fees on drug makers while expanding the insured market that buys their products; repeal would remove both the costs and the larger market.
Repeal would erase the employer mandate penalties and reporting requirements the ACA placed on large firms, at the cost of ending the coverage expansion their employees used.
Repeal would eliminate the ACA's additional Medicare taxes on high earners and large estates, a benefit concentrated at the top of the income scale.
